title: Energy and Maritime Security

cards.b: India imports about 85 per cent of its crude oil and roughly half its gas. Over 90 per cent of its trade by volume moves by sea. Disruption at a chokepoint would hit prices, growth and security alike, which makes energy and maritime security a central Paper II topic.
As of the 2020s, Russia became India's top crude supplier after 2022, which triggered US pressure and tariffs in 2025. India says its energy purchases serve consumer interest and its autonomy.

• Diversify suppliers and routes.
  • Strategic Petroleum Reserves (Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur; about 5.3 million tonnes).
  • Overseas assets: ONGC Videsh in Russia (Sakhalin-1), Mozambique, Brazil.
  • Cross-border pipelines (TAPI, IPI both stalled).
  • Transition: solar (International Solar Alliance, 2015), green hydrogen mission (2023), nuclear targets, ethanol blending.

India's oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz (about a fifth of world oil), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea, Houthi attacks since late 2023) and Malacca. The Indian Navy's Operation Sankalp (2019 on) protects shipping in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf of Aden, and it deployed ships in the Red Sea in 2023-24 after attacks. The Navy is also fighting piracy; the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act (2022) gave it legal powers.

The Indian Maritime Security Strategy (2015, 'Ensuring Secure Seas') and SAGAR set out the Navy's roles: deterrence, coastal security, HADR, and diplomacy. Assets: INS Vikrant (commissioned September 2022), INS Arihant SSBN, Project 75 submarines, Rafale-M. After 26/11 coastal security was reformed (Coastal Security Scheme, 2005; National Committee). India ratified UNCLOS in 1995.

The Quad (Malabar exercise), IPOI (2019), IMEC corridor (announced at the G20 in 2023), the Information Fusion Centre, 2+2 dialogues, logistics agreements (LEMOA 2016) and Colombo Security Conclave. India stresses a rule-based order and freedom of navigation, supporting the 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea.

• Energy autonomy versus sanctions and tariffs from Western partners.
  • Clean-energy targets versus coal dependence.
  • A strong Navy needs funding (the Army and Air Force receive more).
  • China's Indian Ocean presence and research ships.
  • Blue economy and Sagarmala projects can harm coastal communities and the environment.

Maritime security includes fisheries, deep-sea mining (India's Deep Ocean Mission, 2021), ports (Sagarmala, 2015) and shipping. The Blue Economy policy aims to turn the ocean into a development resource, using ideas of sustainable use. This links energy, trade and security as one system.

Priorities: expand reserves, speed up renewables and storage, build domestic shipbuilding, keep multi-vector supplies, and invest in maritime domain awareness. In answers, link energy to strategic autonomy and link the sea to the Indo-Pacific vision. Also tie to GS III energy and infrastructure.
